ket_qua.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote covers roughly one hectare, about the size of two soccer fields.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: National Geographic (2017) says about one hectare, roughly two soccer fields (about 12,000 sq yd); Radio Nacional and Voz de America say just over one hectare. Other estimates range from 1.2 ha (El Pais via Wikipedia) to 1.57 ha (Red Prensa Verde), so 'roughly' is appropriate.

ket_qua.statement: Media reports often describe Santa Cruz del Islote as one of the most densely populated islands in the world; the claim depends on population estimates that vary widely.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: NatGeo, CNN, The Guardian, BBC Mundo and others call it the most crowded or densely populated island; population figures in reputable outlets range from about 500 to 1,300, and the DANE census counted 432 in 2018, so the hedge is needed.

ket_qua.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote is surrounded by larger islands of the San Bernardo archipelago, such as Múcura and Tintipán, which have beaches and vegetation including mangroves.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: Tintipán is the largest island in the archipelago and its interior is mangrove swamp; Múcura has the only public beach plus hotel beaches and remaining mangroves (Red Prensa Verde); BBC Mundo notes both have water and farmland.

ket_qua.statement: According to a story told by locals, the fishermen who first settled on Santa Cruz del Islote chose it because it had no mosquitoes.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: CNN (Spanish edition) reports the legend that fishermen stayed after finding no mosquitoes; BBC Mundo says residents cite the absence of mosquitoes as a key reason the settlers built there; Radio Nacional tells the same story about the jején. All present it as local lore.

ket_qua.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote is about a two-hour boat ride from Cartagena, Colombia.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: National Geographic, Noticias RCN and Radio Nacional all give about two hours by boat from Cartagena.

ket_qua.ghi_chu: Noticias RCN: 'a una hora del municipio de Tolú en lancha'; Radio Nacional: about one hour from San Onofre and Tolú (some travel guides say 45 minutes).

ket_qua.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote has around 100 mostly one-storey houses, a school, a restaurant and a small square with a cross that gives the island its name, and no roads or cars.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: School, restaurant (VOA), central cross that gave the name and no roads (NatGeo) are supported, but the house count varies widely: 97 (NatGeo 2017), about 100 (Lindblad), 115 (CNN 2018), 120 (ABC Economía 2019), about 140 (VOA), about 160 (Radio Nacional); 'mostly one-storey' has no strong source and several outlets say families are building second floors, so hedge or say 'more than a hundred'.

ket_qua.statement: About 150 years ago Santa Cruz del Islote was a small uninhabited island that fishermen from Cartagena and Tolú used to rest and to shelter from storms.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: NatGeo (2017, quoting photographer Charlie Cordero) gives about 150 years ago, uninhabited, used by fishermen from Cartagena and Tolú to rest and shelter from storms; BBC Mundo (2018) dates settlement to 1870. Radio Nacional's outlier says about 200 years.

ket_qua.ghi_chu: CNN: locals credit the insect-free environment to the absence of mangroves and beaches; BBC Mundo: no mangroves or beaches, so no mosquitoes; VOA confirms the island has no beaches. No scientific confirmation, so keep it as locals' explanation.

ket_qua.statement: On Santa Cruz del Islote, the Pintuco Foundation and the Colombian Navy repainted the house facades, and nine murals were created together with the community.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: ABC Economía (5 Mar 2019): 'La Fundación Pintuco, junto con la Armada Nacional, pintó todas las fachadas' and 'nueve murales en co-creación con la comunidad'. It is the only source found (likely based on a press release); no Pintuco or Navy page was found.

ket_qua.statement: Fishing remains the main livelihood on Santa Cruz del Islote, although tourism is growing.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: La Nación (2026): fishing is still the 'principal sustento' while tourism grows; BBC Mundo and Radio Nacional: residents live from fishing and tourism.

ket_qua.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote has no natural fresh water source, and the Colombian Navy has delivered drinking water by boat to communities in the San Bernardo archipelago including Santa Cruz del Islote.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: NatGeo: drinking water can't be produced on the island and the Navy delivered it; La Nación and BBC Mundo: rainwater cistern, and a Navy ship brings water from Cartagena; Colombian military (CGFM, Apr 2024): over 168,000 litres delivered to Santa Cruz del Islote and other islands with support from the ARC Golfo de Morrosquillo.

ket_qua.statement: In 2021 Colombia's Ministry of Mines and Energy delivered a hybrid solar-diesel power plant to Santa Cruz del Islote, including a new 125 kVA diesel generator and maintenance of its battery bank.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: El Heraldo (22 Oct 2021) frames it as MinMinas/IPSE delivering hybrid plants to three islands, but for the Islote it lists only a new 125 kVA diesel plant, an inverter, and maintenance of the battery bank and electronics. IPSE already reported a working system there in 2016 (Energías Renovables), and Radio Nacional/RCN say the panels were donated earlier by Japan. 2021 was an upgrade of an existing hybrid system; the narration's 'set up... with solar panels' overstates it.

ket_qua.statement: Tourism is increasingly important to Santa Cruz del Islote; visitors arrive by speedboat from hotels on nearby islands such as Múcura, and some islanders are reported to work at those hotels.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: CNN: tourists stay at the Punta Faro hotel on Múcura and come over by speedboat; BBC Mundo: 'Algunos trabajan en hoteles de las islas vecinas'; La Nación (2026): tourism is growing.

ket_qua.statement: The Guardian reported that residents of the San Bernardo islands sometimes wake to find their homes flooded, and that the archipelago sits on average about 2 metres (about 6.5 feet) above sea level.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: Guardian article by Iñigo Alexander (2023), read via syndicated copies because theguardian.com was blocked: islands 'at an average of only 2 metres (6ft) above the waterline'; on Santa Cruz del Islote residents wake to wet floors and homes can flood at any time (der Freitag). VOA puts Santa Cruz itself at about 1 m.

ket_qua.statement: A 2014 local government report found erosion affecting about 45% of the San Bernardo archipelago's coastlines, and Maravilla Island, about one hectare, had disappeared by around 2017.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: The 2014 report and 45% erosion figure come from the Guardian (2023), and the Guardian also gives Maravilla as 1 ha and gone since 2017. Invemar describes it as a 0.004 km² islet (about 0.4 ha) and, citing Parques Nacionales, dates its loss to 2006-2007; Red Prensa Verde says less than one hectare. 'About a hectare' is disputed; 'a small island' or 'less than a hectare' is safer.

ket_qua.statement: Global sea levels are expected to rise by up to about 30 cm (about one foot) by 2050.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: IPCC AR6 likely range for 2050 global mean sea level rise relative to 1995-2014 is 0.15-0.23 m (SSP1-1.9) up to 0.20-0.29 m (SSP5-8.5), so 'up to about 30 cm' is the top of the range. NOAA's 25-30 cm figure applies to US coastlines, not the globe.

ket_qua.statement: Because of Santa Cruz del Islote's small size, some residents have moved to neighbouring islands such as Tintipán or Múcura, and students who continue their education leave the island.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: Students leaving after grade 10 is supported (NatGeo, Lindblad). The move to Tintipán or Múcura is not: Spanish Wikipedia cites BBC Mundo, but BBC Mundo says islanders refused to move to Tintipán or Múcura. Only Red Prensa Verde mentions Islote natives occupying lots on nearby islands. Keep only the students part, or hedge.
